name: Von Baer's Laws
statement: Embryos of related animals start alike and diverge, resembling each other's embryos, never each other's adults.
meaning: Development proceeds from the general to the special. The broad features shared by a large group appear in the embryo before the traits that distinguish species, so embryos of related animals look alike early on and progressively diverge. A mammal embryo resembles a fish embryo, never an adult fish — development branches apart rather than climbing a ladder of ancestral adult forms.
mechanism: Ontogeny runs as a branching divergence, not a linear march. Generalised, broadly shared body features form first; increasingly specialised, group-specific and then species-specific structures form later. Because each embryo becomes separated from the others as it specialises rather than passing through their forms, the resemblance between related animals is greatest at the earliest stages and diminishes as development proceeds. Individual structures appear in sequence, not whole ancestral organisms.

examples.text: Human, fish, and chick embryos look strongly alike in early development, sharing general vertebrate features, then progressively diverge as species-specific traits appear.

Early human embryos have structures resembling gill slits; von Baer argued these resemble only the embryonic structures of fish, not adult fish — a direct illustration of embryos resembling embryos, not ancestral adults.
The broad characters of a large group emerge in the embryo before the special characters, so what an embryo is destined to become narrows step by step from group to species.

variants.name: The developmental hourglass
variants.text: The modern refinement: vertebrate embryos are most alike not at the very start but at a mid-development phylotypic stage, with more variation both before and after — modifying von Baer's emphasis on earliest similarity.

variants.name: Haeckel's recapitulation
variants.text: The later, opposed theory that von Baer's laws contradict — Haeckel's 1866 claim that embryos replay ancestral adult stages, an idea von Baer's account predates and refutes.

whyItMatters: They are a foundational contribution to embryology and a more accurate account of development than the recapitulation theory that later overshadowed them in popular imagination. Based on direct comparative observation, the core insight — general before special, embryos resembling embryos — is still taught and broadly upheld, refined rather than overturned.

working.lead: Read early likeness as shared generality
working.text: when related embryos look alike, see shared general features, not a replay of ancestral adults.
when an embryonic structure resembles another animal, match it to that animal's embryo, not its adult form.
expect maximal similarity at a mid-development phylotypic stage rather than strictly at the earliest moment.

limits: The laws are largely upheld but refined by modern evolutionary developmental biology. The developmental hourglass shows embryos of a phylum are most conserved at a mid-development phylotypic stage, not strictly at the earliest, so 'earliest equals most similar' is not literally exact in every ordering. They must be sharply distinguished from Haeckel's recapitulation theory, which they oppose and which is discredited; Haeckel's exaggerated embryo drawings are sometimes wrongly used to discredit embryology in general, but they do not implicate von Baer's observation-based laws.
misreadings: They are the opposite of the popular 'ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny' — von Baer said embryos resemble other embryos, never ancestral adults, and framed his laws specifically to refute recapitulation. And they are not exact in every detail: development is most conserved at a middle stage, a modern refinement rather than a contradiction.
origin: Set out by Karl Ernst von Baer in 1828 at the University of Konigsberg, in Uber Entwickelungsgeschichte der Thiere ('On the Developmental History of Animals'), formulated to discredit the recapitulation idea earlier proposed by Johann Friedrich Meckel and predating Haeckel's biogenetic law of 1866.
